Hi everyone, I'm the maker of Siteprint. [...] Filip Papic

Hi everyone, I'm the maker of Siteprint.

I'll be upfront: tools that generate design prompts and pull colors, fonts from a website aren't new, and Chrome has dozens of them. But I spend my day in Safari, and I wanted one that feels at home there instead of switching browsers. So I built it as a proper Safari extension.

Being a Safari extension also brings a built-in upgrade: Apple Intelligence. On a Mac that has it, the on-device model reviews each scan, names its colors and type styles, describes the feel and what to keep or avoid, and answers your questions about the design. On a Mac without it, everything measured works just the same.

results.title: What We're Learning from HP SitePrint
results.content:
The robot does not understand design intent. It cannot recognize an outdated drawing, determine whether two trades are coordinated, or tell us that the model does not match current field conditions. If we give it incorrect information, it will print that information very efficiently. The responsibility for verifying it still belongs to us. [...] I recently used HP SitePrint to complete layout across approximately 5,000 SF, including walls and overhead lighting, in roughly two hours. I operated it by myself, and the production was impressive. But the most important work happened before the robot printed its first line.  
  
At its core, I think of SitePrint as a highly advanced prism pole and chalk box. We load the prepared design information into the system, use a robotic total station to track its position, and have the robot print the selected linework directly on the floor. It is fast, but it only puts down the information we give it, whether that information is good or bad. [...] HP SitePrint is a robotic layout system that prints digital design information directly onto the jobsite floor. We are piloting it to understand where it creates value, what preparation it requires, and how it supports field engineers’ work. Here’s what we’ve learned so far.

Fast Printing Starts with Good Information
